title: The fletcher (33–34)
hookLine: the wise straighten the trembling mind as a fletcher straightens an arrow; the mind flaps like a fish on dry land
last: THE RACEHORSE — AWAKE AMONG THE SLEEPING.

lines: EASE THE BEND, NEVER SNAP IT.
cards: Before factories, arrows were made by hand, one at a time, by a craftsman called a fletcher. The hard part wasn't the feathers or the point. It was the shaft.

A length of cane or wood is never quite straight. So the fletcher would warm it gently over a fire, sight down its length, find the bend, and ease it true, a little at a time, between his hands or in a notched tool.
Then sight again, and ease again. Patient, careful, never snapping it. The Dhammapada says the wise do exactly that with something else.

teach.b: Chapter three is called citta, which Müller translates thought. Citta is one of the Pali words for mind: the heart-mind that thinks, feels and wants, all at once.
Verse thirty-three: “As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.”
Trembling and unsteady: not a calm mind that needs a little polish, but one that shakes.
Verse thirty-four gives the picture: “As a fish taken from his watery home and thrown on the dry ground, our thought trembles all over.”
Anyone who's watched a fish on a dock knows that flapping: frantic, desperate, going nowhere. That's the mind pulled out of its old habits; it wants to jump back in.
The commentary tells these verses about Meghiya, a monk who was attending the Buddha.
He saw a beautiful mango grove and asked to go and meditate there. The Buddha asked him to wait. He asked again, and again, and finally the Buddha let him go.
In the grove, Meghiya's mind was flooded with thoughts of desire, anger and harm, and he came back shaken, flapping like the fish. So the verses don't pretend this is easy.
They name the difficulty, and then they give a craft.
Not force: the fletcher never snaps the shaft. Warmth, patience, find the bend, ease it true, sight again. That's also a fair description of the sitting you've been doing for months.

how: Buddhist meditation teachers often use the fletcher image to describe training the mind patiently, and the chapter on citta is taught as a guide to working with the mind.

o: an unchanging soul that lives on after the body dies
the heart-mind that thinks, feels and wants all at once
the reasoning brain, kept separate from all feeling

games.q: match the pictures of chapter three.
p: went to the mango grove too soon

s: the fletcher verse assumes the mind starts out calm
it starts with a mind that is trembling and unsteady, hard to guard.
in the commentary, Meghiya's mind was flooded with troubling thoughts in the mango grove
he went before he was ready and came back shaken.
citta means only the thinking part of the mind
it's the heart-mind: thinking, feeling and wanting together.

games.q: you're Meghiya. you see a beautiful mango grove and ask the Buddha if you can go and meditate there. he asks you to wait. what do you do?
o: keep asking until he lets you go.
games.why: Meghiya asked three times and went. in the grove his mind was flooded with desire, anger and harm, and he came back shaken.

practice: Let the breath be the fire that warms the shaft, and sight down the mind: a worry leaning one way, an irritation pulling another, a plan that won't let go.
Pick one bent thought; don't wrench it, just see it clearly and let the next breath ease it a little, less tight, closer to true. If it springs back, that's normal: sight again, ease again.

wordCard.voice: Citta. The mind, or heart-mind: trembling and unsteady at first, and made straight by patient work, like an arrow.

orig.note: Pali: mind, heart-mind, the title of chapter three.

carryVoice: Your line: straighten the arrow. Warmth and patience, a little at a time, never force. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
As a fish taken from his watery home and thrown on the dry ground, our thought trembles all over

sources.ref: Udana 4.1 (Meghiya Sutta); Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of Meghiya Thera (verses 33–34)
